Multi-omics has moved from a methodological aspiration to a routine design choice in molecular biology, and the conceptual rationale is no longer in dispute: simultaneous profiling of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbial layers captures interactions that no single assay can resolve [R1, R54]. What has lagged behind this conceptual maturation, however, is the software infrastructure that researchers must actually use. A typical multi-omics project now involves five to seven data types, several thousand samples and a downstream pipeline that spans preprocessing, integration, dimensionality reduction, clustering, biomarker discovery and visualisation. Each of those steps admits a dozen or more competing implementations, and the tooling has accumulated faster than the standards that should govern it. The result is an analytical gap that is no longer conceptual but infrastructural: researchers spend more time reconciling file formats, harmonising object classes and reproducing someone else's R environment than they do interpreting biological signal.

The heterogeneity of the available tools is striking. On the R side, Bioconductor provides the foundational data structures, most notably MultiAssayExperiment, which offers coordinated representation, storage and operation on diverse genomics datasets and ships with ready-to-analyse TCGA objects [R28]; on top of this substrate the community has built package-specific integrators such as mixOmics with its DIABLO supervised framework [R27], the longitudinal timeOmics [R20] and netOmics packages [R21], the vertical and horizontal miodin workflow [R48], the MOFA-based transfer-learning extension MOTL [R32], the MuSA radiogenomic GUI built on the same MultiAssayExperiment class [R25], and reproducibility-oriented wrappers such as moiraine that let users compare multiple integrators head-to-head [R3]. The Python ecosystem is no less crowded, ranging from graph-neural-network frameworks such as BioNeuralNet [R5] to specialised deep-learning integrators including MOADLN [R17], MCluster-VAEs [R22], MO-GCAN [R29], DeepMoIC [R12] and MoAGL-SA [R39]. Parallel to these programmatic ecosystems, web-based point-and-click platforms have proliferated: the Analyst suite (ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet, OmicsAnalyst) [R8], ExpOmics [R41], the single-cell analyst [R6], CFViSA [R40], NOODAI [R33], PhenoMultiOmics [R14] and disease-specific portals such as CPMOAD [R7] and LOSTdb [R34] now offer GUI-driven alternatives that lower the barrier to entry but introduce their own concerns about transparency and reproducibility. Finally, containerised, workflow-management approaches — Nextflow, Snakemake and WorkflowHub-compatible Research Object Crates [R11, R18, R26, R35] — attempt to capture provenance at the level of the analysis environment itself.

Among these application domains, host–microbiome research exemplifies the infrastructural pressure particularly acutely. Microbial community samples bring together metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics, with sample coverage that is intrinsically inconsistent across layers because taxa differ in their genomic recoverability, expression detectability and chemical extractability [R1, R54]. As the microbial multi-omics perspective of Van Den Bossche and colleagues emphasises, the complexity of analysing a single isolate is multiplied further when samples comprise hundreds to thousands of individual species, yet standardised workflows and benchmarked datasets remain scarce [R54]. This combination — heterogeneous data formats, inconsistent sample coverage, complex analytical chains and weak reproducibility standards — is precisely what motivated the development of workflow-level solutions such as EasyMultiProfiler (EMP), an R workflow built on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment that organises extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation into a single coherent pipeline [R1]. Microbiome multi-omics is therefore not just another application area; it is a canonical stress test for any claim that multi-omics software has matured as an infrastructure.

A candid assessment must temper the cataloguing instinct. The sheer number of tools is often taken as evidence of progress, yet the evidence reviewed here describes a field in which each new publication tends to add another integration method rather than consolidate best practice. Benchmarking studies of cancer subtype clustering [R4], multi-omics biomarker discovery [R50] and single-cell integration [R10, R37] consistently find that no single method dominates across datasets, and that gains over simpler baselines are often modest. The persistence of batch effects, platform-specific artefacts and the absence of agreed-upon reference datasets mean that methodological choice — not biological signal — frequently determines the headline result. Tool catalogues lengthen faster than standards mature, and the fragmentation that integration was meant to solve remains, in many respects, intact. The review that follows takes this tension as its starting point: it surveys the available software landscape across general-purpose frameworks, microbiome-centred tools, GUI platforms and containerised infrastructure, examines the limited but informative benchmarking evidence, and uses EasyMultiProfiler as a worked example of what a domain-specific, workflow-level solution can — and cannot — deliver relative to its alternatives.

A useful organising principle for the heterogeneous landscape of multi-omics integration software is the point in the analytical pipeline at which information from different omics layers is allowed to interact. Three regimes are routinely distinguished in the methodological literature: early integration, in which raw or preprocessed features from each omics layer are concatenated into a single matrix and fed to one downstream learner; intermediate integration, in which each omics is first summarised in its own representation and the resulting views are then fused in a joint latent space, graph, or factor decomposition; and late integration, in which omics-specific models are trained independently and their outputs are combined only at the decision or prediction stage. This taxonomy, while inevitably simplified, maps cleanly onto the principal algorithmic families represented in the corpus reviewed here, and it provides a frame against which claims of methodological novelty can be assessed.

Early integration remains the most straightforward strategy and the easiest to implement on top of generic machine-learning toolkits. In its classical form it underlies pipelines that learn patient embeddings or disease classifiers directly from concatenated feature vectors. The MOADLN framework, for instance, uses three fully connected layers per omics and a self-attention module to reduce dimensionality before concatenating the views for downstream classification [R17]. The contrastive adversarial encoder CAEncoder similarly treats the integrated matrix as input to a Vision Transformer trained end-to-end against a CycleGAN-based adversarial objective [R30]. Conceptual schemes such as STATegra formalise early integration through a non-parametric data-combination step that follows a per-omics machine-learning component analysis [R24]. The appeal of this regime lies in its simplicity and in its compatibility with any supervised learner; its principal weaknesses, by contrast, are the curse of dimensionality when omics blocks differ in scale and the implicit assumption that cross-omics interactions can be captured by a single monolithic model.

Intermediate integration has become the dominant paradigm in bulk and single-cell multi-omics research. The most influential instances are joint matrix-factorisation methods and similarity-based fusion algorithms. The MOFA family and its transfer-learning extension MOTL exemplify the factor-analytic branch, projecting each omics into a shared low-dimensional space whose factors can be annotated biologically and used for downstream clustering or regression [R32]. Similarity network fusion and its descendants constitute a parallel branch that constructs per-omics patient graphs and iteratively fuses them into a single affinity matrix; in the recent benchmarking of eight representative early, intermediate and late integration methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data, SNF emerged as the strongest performer on both simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. A more recent wave of intermediate methods adds deep representation learning to this template. DeepMoIC uses autoencoders to obtain compact per-omics embeddings and then incorporates a patient similarity network through a graph-convolutional architecture [R12]; MCluster-VAEs employs a unified variational autoencoder with an attention mechanism to learn cluster-friendly representations in an end-to-end fashion [R22]; MoAGL-SA generates patient graphs from each omics with graph learning and uses self-attention to weight per-omics graph embeddings adaptively before classification [R39]; MO-GCAN combines per-omics graph convolutional networks with a sample-fusion graph attention network for supervised subtyping across eight cancer types [R29]; and TMODINET adds a Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation head to a self-attention and graph-convolutional backbone to address the trustworthiness of predictions in clinical settings [R9]. The supervised feature-selection framework DIABLO from the mixOmics package sits at the boundary of intermediate and supervised integration, since it constructs sparse latent components that are jointly predictive of phenotypic groups while remaining interpretable as correlated biomarker signatures [R27].

Late integration, in which each omics produces its own prediction that is then aggregated, is conceptually the most modular and the least prone to dominance by the highest-variance view. Software-side support for late fusion is less conspicuous than for the other two regimes, but it is implicitly used whenever pipelines train separate per-omics classifiers or survival models and combine them at the score level, as in parts of the multi-omics biomarker benchmark that compared 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods across five cancer datasets [R50]. The reduced representation of each omics to a prediction score also makes late integration attractive when cohorts are partially overlapping and omics blocks differ in availability.

A second axis that cuts orthogonally across this pipeline taxonomy is the degree of supervision. Unsupervised methods dominate the discovery-oriented literature, where the goal is subtype identification, dimensionality reduction or biomarker prioritisation without external labels; representative tools include SNF [R4], MOFA and MOTL [R32], MCluster-VAEs [R22] and the CancerSubtypes package that wraps four unsupervised subtype-discovery approaches with standardised preprocessing [R49]. Supervised methods, in turn, are preferred when gold-standard endpoints such as cancer subtype, drug response or survival are available; DIABLO [R27], MOADLN [R17], MO-GCAN [R29], TMODINET [R9] and the survival-prediction benchmark that evaluated 11 methods across 18 TCGA datasets [R46] all belong to this category. The systematic survival benchmark is notable because it reported that only one of the multi-omics methods, block forest, outperformed a clinical Cox model, providing one of the few head-to-head empirical demonstrations that more elaborate integration architectures do not always yield better predictions than simpler baselines [R46].

Single-cell multimodal integration adds a third dimension to this scheme because it must reconcile modalities measured on the same cell, on matched cells across modalities, or on different cells within a population. The benchmark of 14 protein-abundance prediction algorithms and 18 single-cell integration algorithms on 47 datasets found totalVI and scArches to be the top protein predictors and Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI to be the strongest vertical integrators [R10], while a parallel benchmark of 12 multi-omics integration methods on RNA and ATAC data emphasised that no single method dominates across the six evaluation aspects considered [R37]. Domain-specific tools such as scMGAT for joint RNA, protein, methylation and ATAC integration [R51] and ScSmOP for single-molecule multiomics [R19] further populate this niche.

A critical reading of the literature reveals two persistent limitations of the proposed taxonomy. First, the same architectural template, most prominently the combination of graph attention networks with per-omics encoders, is re-instantiated with minor variations across cancers, omics combinations and prediction tasks [R12, R29, R39, R42, R51], and the accompanying papers typically demonstrate improvement over a small, often self-curated, baseline set rather than over state-of-the-art supervised or factor-analytic methods evaluated under matched conditions. Second, claims about the superiority of early, intermediate or late fusion are rarely supported by rigorous head-to-head evaluation: the CRC benchmark [R4], the survival benchmark [R46], the single-cell integration benchmarks [R10, R37] and the multi-omics biomarker benchmark [R50] all show that the relative ranking of integration strategies is dataset-dependent, and that simpler early or late approaches can be competitive with, or superior to, more elaborate intermediate models in specific settings. The taxonomy is therefore best used as a descriptive device rather than as evidence for any universal methodological hierarchy.

General-purpose integration frameworks can be grouped along a continuum from tools that genuinely abstract the integration step — exposing it as a swappable component in a wider workflow — to packages that hard-wire a single algorithm and treat preprocessing or visualisation as the only configurable layer. The most useful abstractions decouple three concerns: the data container, the integration operator, and the downstream statistical or biological interpretation. The R/Bioconductor ecosystem has been particularly fertile for this style of design. The moiraine package builds reproducible multi-omics pipelines that preprocess heterogeneous omics layers, dispatch them to one or more user-chosen integration methods, and return standardised outputs so that the results can be compared across algorithms [R3]. Similarly, miodin offers a workflow-based syntax in which the same pipeline language supports vertical integration (the same samples profiled on different platforms) and horizontal integration (the same variables measured across studies), allowing transparent re-use of the same analysis scaffolding across transcriptomics, genomics and proteomics [R48]. timeOmics and its companion netOmics extend this philosophy to the temporal and network interpretation domains respectively: timeOmics provides pre-processing, modelling and clustering of longitudinal multi-omics data and was demonstrated on the integrative Human Microbiome Project diabetes dataset combining mRNA, metabolites, gut taxa and clinical variables [R20], while netOmics builds hybrid multi-omics networks with smart node labelling and propagation to extract interpretable relationships from the same kind of data [R21]. These four packages share the property that the integration algorithm is an explicit, named object in the workflow — in other words, the user is not buying a single method but a methodology-neutral execution engine.

A second tier of R packages is method-centric yet still generalisable, exposing a single integrative operator but with rich pre-processing, validation and visualisation surrounding it. mixOmics and its supervised DIABLO extension [R27] form the canonical example, with detailed reproducible workflows demonstrated for plant multi-omics under abiotic stress combining phenomics, metabolomics, proteomics and transcriptomics [R16]. CancerSubtypes packages four established subtype-identification algorithms behind a common interface, allowing feature selection, validation and biological follow-up to be swapped in and out [R49]. MUUMI sits between these tiers: it is presented as a unified R framework for statistical meta-analysis combined with similarity network fusion and molecular interactome inference, but its integration layer is essentially fixed — the value-add is the coupling of meta-analysis to network interpretation rather than algorithm interchangeability [R2]. FindIT2 occupies a more specialised niche, providing a complete framework for TF target inference from ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq and RNA-seq that is highly generalisable across species but constrained to a single biological question [R45]. The Python side is currently less populated by neutral abstraction layers and more by deep-learning frameworks with fixed graph architectures, exemplified by BioNeuralNet, a modular graph neural network framework for end-to-end network-based multi-omics analysis [R5].

It is worth pausing on what the benchmarking literature actually says about the relative merit of these approaches. A large-scale benchmark of 11 survival prediction methods across 18 TCGA multi-omics datasets found that methods explicitly accounting for multi-omics group structure performed only marginally better than naive single-block baselines, and that only the block-forest variant — a tree-based ensemble that respects block boundaries — meaningfully outperformed a clinical Cox model [R46]. The implication is sobering for the deep-learning community: statistical and machine-learning methods (boosting, penalised regression, random forest) implemented with a comparatively small methodological footprint remain competitive with far more elaborate architectures on tabular multi-omics data, and the additional complexity of graph attention, variational autoencoders or cycleGAN-based encoders is rarely justified by accuracy alone on cancer benchmarks [R4, R50]. This observation does not invalidate the deep models, but it suggests that the methodological footprint of a framework is a poor proxy for its predictive value.

Several limitations cut across this whole class of tools. First, the abstraction layers — moiraine, miodin, timeOmics — are R-centric, which makes them composable with the Bioconductor infrastructure (MultiAssayExperiment, SummarizedExperiment) but more difficult to weave into Python ecosystems that increasingly dominate deep-learning for omics. Second, the more specialised packages such as MUUMI, CancerSubtypes or the NMF-plus-metaheuristic framework combining adaptive gorilla troops optimisation with sparse-joint NMF for cancer subtyping [R43] often lack head-to-head comparisons against the very algorithms they are intended to complement, so claims of added value rest on demonstration rather than systematic benchmarking. Third, most frameworks are validated on a small number of case studies (IPF transcriptomes and THP-1 macrophages for MUUMI [R2]; Arabidopsis stress data for the mixOmics workflow [R16]; iHMP diabetes for timeOmics [R20]; TCGA glioblastoma and melanoma for the STATegra conceptual framework [R24]), which limits generalisability claims. A critical user, therefore, should weigh a framework's abstraction level, its algorithmic bias, and the breadth of empirical evidence behind it rather than relying on its surface feature list.

Microbiome research has long grappled with the gap between taxonomy-oriented surveys and functional understanding of microbial communities. The shift toward host–microbiome multi-omics—where metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics and host-response layers must be jointly analysed—exposes a sobering reality: most tools remain optimised for human cohorts and 16S-derived taxon profiles rather than for the cross-kingdom, functional, and non-model contexts in which microbiomes actually live. Aligning heterogeneous meta-omics layers with host molecular phenotypes is therefore the central unmet challenge that distinguishes microbiome-centred integration from generic cancer or single-cell pipelines, and the tools that do exist are unevenly distributed across the problems they claim to solve.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is positioned explicitly as a microbiome-centric workflow that adopts the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment data structures from Bioconductor to unify storage and analysis across extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation modules [R1]. Its strength is the disciplined decomposition of a multi-step microbiome pipeline into a coherent R-based workflow that reduces methodological inconsistency between meta-omics datasets and improves reproducibility, which the authors themselves identify as a key bottleneck in the field [R1]. EMP's design is well suited to human and mammalian microbiome projects where established reference databases and curated metadata schemas exist. What the publication does not demonstrate, however, is robust performance on non-model host-associated microbiomes or on studies in which metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic signals dominate and reference annotations are sparse. The framework is therefore best understood as a strong template for standardised human host-microbiome research, not yet as a universal solution for cross-kingdom meta-omics integration.

By contrast, gNOMO was built precisely for the underserved non-model organism case, integrating up to three meta-omics levels—metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics—within a Snakemake-managed pipeline demonstrated on the cockroach Blattella germanica gut microbiome [R26]. Its value lies less in statistical novelty than in acknowledging that the absence of well-annotated reference genomes is the rule rather than the exception for invertebrate, environmental and engineered microbiome studies, and that reproducibility tooling must therefore be paired with database-aware assembly and quantification steps [R26]. Notably, gNOMO does not natively incorporate host transcriptomics or metabolomics; cross-kingdom host-microbe alignment remains a manual step, illustrating how far microbiome multi-omics tooling still lags behind host-centric cancer pipelines that benefit from rich TCGA-style resources [R26].

CFViSA takes a complementary, web-based route, offering 79 analytical tools and integrated microbiome and transcriptome pipelines through a point-and-click Scala/AKKA front end backed by R computations [R40]. This lower barrier to entry is attractive for groups without dedicated bioinformatics capacity, but the platform is primarily a statistical and visualisation suite: it does not orchestrate raw metagenomic read assembly, metatranscriptomic mapping or metaproteomic peptide identification, and so the upstream burden of producing coherent meta-omics matrices falls on the user [R40]. As such, CFViSA complements rather than substitutes for dedicated meta-omics engines.

The conceptual roadmaps proposed in recent reviews highlight precisely where these tools underperform. Perspective work on integrating multi-omics technologies to decipher microbiome functions emphasises standardised workflows, FAIR-compliant data objects, benchmarked datasets and community-driven initiatives as prerequisites for credible functional inference [R54], while translational reviews on inflammatory bowel disease argue that gut-microbiota-centred multi-omics must move beyond taxonomic dysbiosis signatures toward quantitative, longitudinally validated, action-linked biomarkers [R58]. Neither roadmap is yet operationally realised by existing microbiome-centred tools, and the available evidence does not establish whether any of them can recover known host–microbe mechanisms from integrated meta-omics in a head-to-head, community-accepted benchmark.

In sum, the microbiome-centred segment of the integration landscape is characterised by uneven coverage: EMP offers a reproducible backbone for human host-microbiome studies [R1], gNOMO pioneers non-model meta-omics reproducibility [R26], and CFViSA democratises downstream statistics [R40], but the field still over-relies on 16S-derived taxonomy, lacks a unified engine for functional meta-omics across kingdoms, and has no consensus benchmark for evaluating these workflows. The most consequential limitation across the board is that none of these tools has been independently demonstrated to outperform alternatives on a shared, functionally annotated meta-omics testbed, leaving their relative accuracy largely an open question.

The browser-accessible tier of multi-omics software has expanded substantially over the past five years, in part because dedicated web platforms shield end-users from installation burdens, environment management and version drift. The most mature general-purpose example is the Analyst suite, in which ExpressAnalyst and MetaboAnalyst handle per-omics normalisation and univariate statistics, OmicsNet performs knowledge-driven integration through biological networks, and OmicsAnalyst conducts data-driven integration through joint dimensionality reduction; the suite was demonstrated on a human pancreatic islet transcriptomics, proteomics and lipidomics study, and the individual components are described as fully functional standalone resources usable independently [R8]. Comparable breadth is offered by ExpOmics, which combines seven applications and four toolkits exposing 28 customizable analysis functions—including differential expression, co-expression, WGCNA, feature selection and functional enrichment—across genes, mRNAs, lncRNAs, miRNAs, circRNAs, piRNAs and proteins without organism restriction, and which additionally pre-loads 22,427 TCGA transcriptomic datasets for browsing [R41]. A more focused but still general resource is CFViSA, which integrates 79 analysis tools spanning sequence processing, visualisation and statistical analysis for microbiome and transcriptome data behind a unified web interface [R40]. These platforms demonstrate that genuine analytical depth can be achieved without writing code, but they also expose an inherent tension: the same menu that enables rapid exploration simultaneously constrains users to a curated catalogue of methods and parameters.

Single-cell-focused web platforms have proliferated because the algorithmic complexity of scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, CyTOF and spatial workflows is particularly daunting for non-computational users. The single-cell analyst is illustrative: it supports six single-cell omics types plus spatial transcriptomics, automates QC, processing and phenotype-specific analyses, and exposes over 20 interactive visualisations in both online and offline modes [R6]. The trade-off is that the algorithmic choices—normalisation strategy, dimensionality reduction method, clustering resolution—are baked into the workflow; users receive polished outputs but typically cannot swap in alternative implementations without returning to a command-line tool.

Disease-specific databases represent the most curated end of the spectrum, in which pre-computed cohorts and harmonised annotations substitute for any user-side data processing. CPMOAD uniformly integrates RNA-seq, DNA methylation and curated molecular interaction records for preeclampsia, providing interactive differential expression, methylation and pathway enrichment modules against a preprocessed backbone [R7]. LOSTdb goes further by manually curating 295 multi-omics datasets—bulk RNA-seq, genomic, proteomic, methylation and scRNA-seq—across 34,393 samples and over 1.2 million single cells, and by annotating each sample with both literature-based classical subtypes and NMF-derived meta-program subtypes [R34]. The clear strength of such resources is the elimination of upstream processing decisions and the ability to query across many studies at once. The equally clear weakness is curation drift: reference datasets, gene-model annotations and pathway definitions age quickly, and database-style platforms are vulnerable to becoming stale unless the curators commit to continuous re-ingestion of public data and periodic re-versioning of upstream references. Users should therefore treat pre-computed results as starting points rather than definitive answers.

Pathway- and network-oriented visualisation web servers occupy a more specialised niche. PhenoMultiOmics reconstructs enzymatic-reaction-based multi-omics networks linking genes, proteins and metabolites across cancer types and includes biomarker discovery modules for differential expression and pathway enrichment [R14]. NOODAI constructs joint interaction networks from per-omics representative traits and applies the MONET decomposition tool to identify functionally connected modules in clinical multi-omics datasets [R33]. A complementary network integration framework, MINGLE, fuses multi-omics data into a single graph and was applied to glioma heterogeneity [R31]. These platforms excel at producing publication-ready visualisations but, like other GUI tools, fix the underlying graph-construction algorithms and database versions, so reproducing an identical figure in two years' time may require running a different tool.

Radiogenomics and clinical-translational GUIs illustrate the niche where the ease-of-use case is strongest. MuSA is a Shiny-based tool that wraps the MultiAssayExperiment data structure to combine genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and radiomic features in a single interface for breast cancer radiogenomic studies [R25]. MOPAW is a point-and-click graphical workflow hosted on the Cancer Genomics Cloud that automates preprocessing, dimensionality reduction and MOGSA pathway analysis across copy number, transcriptomic, proteomic and phosphoproteomic data [R18]. The Multi-omics Analysis Sandbox Toolkit further lowers the barrier by integrating clinical data with single- and multi-omics datasets and supporting collaborative sharing of analyses and biomarker candidates [R15]. At the visual periphery, R packages such as chromoMap, which interactively plots genomic and multi-omics features onto chromosomal coordinates [R44], and MultiModalGraphics, which annotates scatterplots and heatmaps with fold-changes, p-values and q-values while interoperating with MultiAssayExperiment, limma, voom and iClusterPlus [R52], occupy a hybrid space between scripted analysis and Shiny-style interactivity, sometimes exposed as widgets within larger web platforms.

The cumulative picture is that web servers and GUI tools have compressed the time from raw data to figure enormously, particularly for clinical and disease-focused communities. Four persistent limitations deserve candid acknowledgement. First, the algorithms are frozen: a new method published last month will not appear until the next platform release, and users cannot easily benchmark alternative implementations. Second, methodological transparency is reduced because the wrapper code that links a parameter to an underlying R or Python function is rarely visible. Third, customisation is shallow—new statistical tests, alternative normalisations or non-standard covariates are typically not exposed. Fourth, database-style platforms are subject to curation drift and stale reference sets, so that pre-computed results can lag behind the literature by years [R7, R34]. These limitations are not reasons to avoid GUI tools but rather to position them as appropriate for rapid hypothesis generation and teaching, while reserving command-line workflows such as EasyMultiProfiler [R1] and other programmatic frameworks for confirmatory analyses, novel method development and reproducible pipelines.

The substrate on which analytical tools sit is rarely scrutinised as carefully as the algorithms they run, yet the choice of data structure has profound consequences for downstream reproducibility and interoperability. The MultiAssayExperiment class introduced in the Bioconductor ecosystem has become a de facto coordinating container for the coordinated representation of multiple diverse genomic datasets, providing ready-to-analyse TCGA multi-omics objects that demonstrably reduce obstacles to scalable, reproducible analysis [R28]. The same ecosystem supplies the lower-level SummarizedExperiment class, on which most omics-specific Bioconductor packages depend, and together these two containers underpin most modern R-based multi-omics analysis. MultiAssayExperiment has, for instance, been adopted as the integrative data structure for radiogenomic studies in MuSA, where it is wrapped by a Shiny interface to permit interactive exploration of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and radiomic features within a single coherent object [R25]. The persistence of MultiAssayExperiment across method implementations is a clear illustration of how container design outlives the lifetime of any single integration algorithm.

Visualisation interoperability is tightly coupled to these containers. chromoMap, an R package for the interactive visualisation of chromosomes, accepts genomic-feature and multi-omics annotations and produces publication-ready plots that integrate across genomic coordinates without imposing a particular upstream analysis pipeline [R44]. MultiModalGraphics similarly exposes annotated scatterplots and heatmaps while interoperating natively with MultiAssayExperiment, limma, voom and iClusterPlus, embedding fold-changes, p-values, q-values and standard deviations directly into the graphical output [R52]. Together these packages demonstrate that the Bioconductor visualisation layer can be added onto the MultiAssayExperiment substrate without forcing users to abandon their preferred differential-abundance or factor-analysis tools. EasyMultiProfiler itself relies on this same SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment substrate, drawing on the same long-term investment in container semantics to offer a five-module pipeline for host–microbiome integration [R1].

Outside R, the next layer of reproducibility infrastructure concerns the workflows that wrap these data structures. A particularly instructive example is a multi-omics analysis workflow developed in Nextflow with versioned containers and rich semantic metadata, packaged as a Research Object Crate and shared via WorkflowHub as a FAIR Digital Object; the implementation relies on RO-Crate metadata and explicit versioning of both workflow and container images, allowing the entire childhood-externalising-behaviour case study to be re-executed by a third party with minimal effort [R11]. A complementary approach is illustrated by moiraine, an R package for constructing reproducible multi-omics integration pipelines that pre-processes data, runs one or more integration methods and produces standardised visualisations while simplifying comparison across tools [R3]. The two designs embody a real trade-off: the Nextflow/FAIR Digital Object approach prioritises machine-actionable, language-agnostic reuse at the cost of an additional container orchestration layer, whereas the moiraine approach maximises interoperability with existing Bioconductor tooling but ties the workflow to the R execution environment.

Cloud-based approaches add further variation. An interdisciplinary learning module on Google Cloud implements a transcriptomics and epigenetics integration pipeline that guides users through three analytical submodules, providing reproducibility by tying execution to the cloud environment rather than to a portable container definition [R13]. While such modules ease entry for non-computational researchers and standardise pedagogical experiences, their long-term archival value is more limited than the FAIR Digital Object pattern just described: the platform-specific binding implies that workflows may become inaccessible if the host cloud is re-priced, deprecated or sold. By contrast, the Nextflow-packaged FAIR Digital Object attached to WorkflowHub remains executable on any infrastructure with a Nextflow runtime and the original container images, a more durable form of reproducibility even when the analysis must be rebuilt on heterogeneous hardware.

It is this infrastructural layer, rather than the algorithmic layer, that most determines whether a published integration method continues to be usable years after publication. Yet methodological benchmarking papers overwhelmingly focus on algorithm selection — including extensive comparative studies in colorectal cancer subtyping [R4], single-cell multi-omics integration [R10] and cancer biomarker discovery [R50] — while giving comparatively little attention to container system, metadata standard or persistent identifier assignment. Empirical evidence on multi-omics reproducibility, while not surveyed exhaustively here, consistently flags unevenness across both R and Python ecosystems: R benefits from Bioconductor's release-cycle discipline, whereas many Python tools are still published without an explicit FAIR-Digital-Object equivalent of RO-Crate and depend on ad hoc container specifications. EasyMultiProfiler's decision to anchor itself on the Bioconductor container substrate is, on this reading, a sound investment in long-term reusability; however, the workflow does not currently bundle RO-Crate metadata or a WorkflowHub-compatible Nextflow wrapper, so that its reproducibility depends largely on the maturity of its dependent Bioconductor packages rather than on a self-contained FAIR Digital Object [R1]. Closing that gap would represent a logical next step for the EMP community and, more broadly, for the microbial multi-omics ecosystem.

A growing body of empirical benchmark studies now provides the scaffolding on which claims of "best" integration method rest. For unsupervised molecular subtyping, a recent benchmark of eight early-, intermediate- and late-integration methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data, complemented by simulated multi-omics structures with realistic cross-omic correlations, identified similarity network fusion (SNF) as the top performer across both simulated and real-world settings [R4]. The same study found that deep-learning alternatives such as graph- and attention-based integration methods, including DeepMoIC [R12], MO-GCAN [R29] and MoAGL-SA [R39], were competitive only on specific evaluation axes and were not uniformly superior to SNF, despite the latter being an older, conceptually simpler approach. This lesson is reinforced by independent benchmarks in cancer survival prediction, where methods that explicitly account for the multi-omics group structure achieved only marginally better predictive accuracy than clinical baselines across 18 TCGA cohorts, with block forest as essentially the only algorithm that significantly outperformed a simple Cox model trained on clinical covariates alone [R46]. This body of evidence tempers the enthusiasm with which novel deep architectures are often promoted: in clinically meaningful tasks, sophisticated multi-omics models rarely dominate, and gains over carefully tuned clinical predictors are frequently marginal.

The single-cell multi-omics benchmark landscape is more nuanced. A systematic evaluation of 14 protein-abundance/chromatin-accessibility prediction algorithms and 18 multi-omics integration algorithms across 47 single-cell datasets reported that totalVI and scArches dominated protein-imputation tasks, whereas Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI led vertical (same-cell) integration, and totalVI and UINMF were best for horizontal/mosaic integration [R10]. A complementary benchmark of 12 methods on three integration tasks for paired single-cell RNA and ATAC data concluded that different methods have their own advantages on different aspects rather than identifying a universal winner [R37]. These are methodologically honest findings, but they expose a deeper problem: benchmarks that exhaustively catalogue per-method strengths implicitly assume that the practitioner can match task to algorithm, and they do not address whether the best-performing methods in benchmark conditions retain their advantage when applied to new cohorts with different batch structures, cell-type compositions or noise profiles. In short, the benchmarks demonstrate clear leadership in specific niches without resolving whether such leadership generalises beyond the curated training cohorts.

A particularly pointed set of concerns arises from the biomarker-discovery literature. A benchmark of 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning multi-omics biomarker identification methods, evaluated against curated gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers across five cancer datasets, found that the top performers, DeePathNet and DeepKEGG, owe much of their advantage to the explicit integration of biological prior knowledge and global feature interactions [R50]. Crucially, many deep-learning methods that achieved high classification accuracy failed to recover clinically actionable biomarkers, and the rankings by predictive accuracy diverged sharply from the rankings by biomarker-recovery fidelity. This dissociation between accuracy and interpretability is not merely an academic concern: regulators and clinicians require named, mechanistically traceable features, and the benchmark implies that the most accurate black-box models are often the least suitable for translation. Independent reviews of deep learning in tumour genomics have reached a similar conclusion, emphasising the need for explainable AI and federated approaches to bridge the accuracy–translation gap [R56].

Across these benchmarks the field lacks a unified evaluation panel, which makes cross-study comparison hazardous. Different studies use different combinations of silhouette scores, normalised mutual information, the concordance index, area under the precision-recall curve, biomarker overlap with gold standards and stability under resampling. Each metric captures a distinct aspect of method behaviour — clustering compactness, agreement with ground-truth labels, discrimination of censored outcomes, biological plausibility, robustness — and no single score summarises "good integration." A direct consequence is that the same method can rank first by silhouette and tenth by NMI on identical data, with no principled basis for choosing one ordering over the other. Benchmarks also differ in their reliance on synthetic versus real data; simulated cohorts tend to favour the integration strategies whose assumptions they encode, whereas real-world TCGA or single-cell datasets reward robustness to noise and confounders [R4, R46]. Reproducible benchmarking infrastructures — including dedicated pipelines for method comparison such as moiraine [R3], FAIR-packaged workflows [R11], and emerging microbiome-specific multi-omics standards [R54] — are beginning to address this gap, but the community still has no accepted reference panel analogous to the standardised assays that structured kinase-inhibitor development. Until such a panel exists, claims that any single method "wins" the integration problem should be read with caution, and the practical recommendation is to interpret benchmark rankings as task-specific evidence rather than as universal endorsements.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is positioned as a streamlined R workflow for host-microbiome multi-omics integration and is built directly on the Bioconductor data-class ecosystem that anchors the field [R1]. Its architecture organises the entire analytical life-cycle into five interconnected modules — data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation — each tied to SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment containers that have become the de facto standard for coordinated handling of multi-assay data in R [R1, R28]. In practice, EMP behaves less as a new statistical engine and more as a curated wrapper that exposes a natural-language-style interface around this data infrastructure, enabling users to assemble microbiome cohorts, host transcriptomes and metabolite profiles into a single MultiAssayExperiment object and to dispatch them to established methods without having to wrangle disparate input formats [R1]. The explicit aim is reproducibility and standardisation in a domain in which inconsistent sample coverage, heterogeneous file formats and bespoke in-house pipelines have repeatedly eroded reliability [R1].

The decision to anchor the workflow in SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment has clear practical consequences. It allows EMP to inherit the coordinated representation, column-wise operation and subsetting semantics documented for the underlying Bioconductor package [R28], and to interoperate with the wider ecosystem of R/Bioconductor tools that already consume these classes. Compared with the general-purpose R integration packages moiraine [R3], miodin [R48] and timeOmics [R20], EMP makes a different design bet: moiraine focuses on reproducibility across multiple competing integration algorithms and explicitly automates the formatting required for each method [R3]; miodin provides a workflow-based syntax for both vertical and horizontal integration across transcriptomic, genomic and proteomic assays [R48]; and timeOmics contributes dedicated longitudinal modelling and clustering for time-resolved multi-omics, demonstrated on integrative Human Microbiome Project data [R20]. EMP does not attempt to replace these contributions; rather, it offers a microbiome-oriented orchestration layer that, in the absence of a head-to-head benchmark, appears to trade breadth of mathematical machinery for ease of cohort assembly and reporting in studies where the central question is host-microbiome interaction [R1].

Against microbiome-specific tools, the most informative comparison is with gNOMO, a Snakemake-based pipeline for integrated metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics from non-model organisms [R26]. gNOMO excels at the upstream, sequence-derived layers of microbiome data and at reproducible workflow management on non-model systems [R26], but it does not natively ingest host-side omics alongside microbial layers in a unified Bioconductor class. EMP's emphasis is complementary: it takes already-processed microbiome features and integrates them with host omics inside a single analytical container, an orientation that fits human cohort studies but leaves the deeper meta-omics computational biology to dedicated upstream pipelines [R1]. In a sense, EMP and gNOMO can be viewed as addressing different points along the same methodological axis — upstream meta-omics assembly versus downstream host-microbe integration — and neither subsumes the other.

Versus graphical platforms, EMP must be evaluated on the dimensions of accessibility versus flexibility. MuSA wraps MultiAssayExperiment in a Shiny-based graphical interface aimed at radiogenomic studies, adding imaging-derived features that fall outside EMP's scope [R25]. The broader Analyst suite — comprising ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet and OmicsAnalyst — offers a web-based, code-free environment for single-omics analysis, knowledge-driven network integration and data-driven joint dimensionality reduction [R8]. These platforms excel at lowering the entry barrier and at providing interactive visualisation, but they typically require data upload to external servers, offer limited algorithmic transparency, and are constrained by the analyses pre-implemented in the web backend. EMP retains the transparency and extensibility of R while constraining users to the Bioconductor release cycle and to locally reproducible execution [R1, R28]. This is a meaningful trade-off: reproducible, scripted analysis with version-controlled dependencies on the one hand, and high accessibility with hidden computational choices on the other.

The critical assessment of EMP must be candid. Its primary value proposition is the standardised five-module wrapper around an established data-class ecosystem, not a novel integration mathematics; new methodological contributions are therefore modest when measured against packages such as DIABLO within mixOmics [R27], MOFA, network-fusion-based methods [R4] or the rapidly expanding family of deep-learning integrators [R5, R12]. Its limitations are also clear. First, EMP is currently scoped to host-microbiome cohorts and does not natively support cross-kingdom meta-omics layers such as metatranscriptomic or metaproteomic assembly, leaving a gap that gNOMO fills for non-model systems [R26]. Second, its tight coupling to Bioconductor classes means that its feature set is paced by Bioconductor release cycles, which can lag behind community-driven methods distributed through CRAN, PyPI or GitHub. Third, EMP is not designed for single-cell multi-omics integration, where dedicated benchmarking has identified very different top performers (e.g., totalVI, scArches, Seurat, MOJITOO, scAI) [R10], nor for radiomic or imaging-augmented integration, where MuSA has a clear head start [R25]. The underlying evidence does not demonstrate that EMP outperforms any specific integration algorithm; what it does demonstrate is that, for the host-microbiome use case, a coherent, class-coordinated wrapper can materially reduce the engineering overhead of assembling reproducible multi-omics analyses [R1]. Positioned this way, EMP is best understood as an integration of ecosystems rather than an integration of omics layers in the methodological sense.

A central controversy in current multi-omics methodology is whether the proliferation of deep learning architectures delivers meaningful advances over classical statistical frameworks, or whether it represents incremental architectural variation over a common encoder-decoder template. Trustworthiness-focused proposals such as TMODINET illustrate the field's stated ambitions: combining self-attention, graph convolutional components and Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation to address calibration and interpretability in cancer diagnostics [R9]. The appeal of calibrated, interpretable predictions in high-stakes clinical settings is obvious, yet many recent methods pair attention with graph convolutional networks in essentially interchangeable configurations, and their claimed gains over supervised regularised regression are often within the noise envelope seen in independent benchmarking [R9, R46, R50]. Large survival-prediction benchmarks across TCGA datasets have repeatedly shown that methods explicitly modelling multi-omics group structure offer only marginal improvements, and that a clinical Cox model is rarely outperformed decisively [R46]. Similar patterns are emerging in cancer biomarker discovery, where deep architectures identified as top performers in one benchmark often fail to generalise to external cohorts [R50]. The community should therefore treat self-attention plus graph-convolutional combinations with scepticism when external validation, calibration curves and decision-curve analyses are absent; the burden of proof for clinical translation has not shifted simply because the encoder backbone has become more elaborate.

A second frontier concerns resolution. Single-cell multi-omics has moved rapidly from co-profiled RNA and chromatin accessibility towards single-molecule, barcode-indexed assays that also capture spatial localisation [R19, R51]. Pipelines such as ScSmOP illustrate that the bottleneck has shifted from chemistry to the engineering of spaced-seed hashing, deconvolution and reproducible mapping for ligation-based and synthesis-based barcodes [R19]. At the same time, single-cell graph attention methods continue to emerge with limited head-to-head comparison [R51], and benchmarking across 47 single-cell datasets suggests that the practical choice of integration method is still highly task-dependent, with no dominant approach across vertical, horizontal and mosaic integration regimes [R10]. The availability of well-curated evaluation resources and modular single-cell platforms will determine whether the next generation of methods is judged by architectural novelty or by measurable improvements on externally validated tasks [R6, R37].

Beyond cellular resolution, the integration question itself is being redefined. Isoform-level integration recognises that alternative splicing can assign distinct functions to transcripts of the same gene, yet current pipelines rarely exploit isoform-isoform interactions or integrate heterogeneous feature domains convincingly [R36]. Frameworks such as CrossIsoFun attempt to address this with omics-specific graph convolutional encoders, view-correlation discovery and cycleGAN-based feature harmonisation, but the evaluation remains largely retrospective and confined to bulk omics [R36]. Complementary efforts push integration into three-dimensional chromatin space, using topologically associating domains as biologically motivated anchors that respect the genome's regulatory architecture [R23]. InterTADs demonstrates the value of this approach in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where confining integration to TADs yields reproducible differences between normal and malignant cells and biologically interpretable enrichments [R23]. The trajectory from gene-level to isoform-level to TAD-level integration suggests that biological scale, rather than algorithmic sophistication, will be the principal driver of insight, particularly when coupled with targeted TF–target discovery pipelines that use ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and RNA-seq in concert [R45, R47].

Network-based approaches are simultaneously gaining traction as an alternative to embedding-centric deep learning. Random-walk with restart on multilayer heterogeneous networks, exemplified by multiXrank in the COVID-19 setting, propagates signal across omics-derived features and curated knowledge graphs to identify biosignatures associated with specific disease phases [R38]. This family of methods offers mechanistic interpretability that attention-based encoders often lack, but their results depend heavily on the completeness and bias of the underlying knowledge graphs and on how missing edges are penalised. Hybrid platforms that fuse variable selection with graph integration, such as MINGLE for glioma heterogeneity, are beginning to address this, but the field still lacks principled criteria for deciding when a multilayer random walk is preferable to a well-tuned matrix factorisation or a similarity-network fusion approach [R31, R3, R4].

Spatially resolved and clinically integrative applications are emerging as the most ambitious proving grounds. Reviews of immunometabolic heterogeneity at the lung cancer tumour-immune interface synthesise single-cell transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and spatial profiling into resistance-linked metabolic subtypes, but stop short of providing tool-grade infrastructure for reproducible re-analysis [R60]. Habitat radiomics extends conventional radiomics by using AI to define intratumoral subregions whose molecular correlates can, in principle, be mapped to omics profiles [R59]. Likewise, recurrent pregnancy loss research now invokes multi-omics stratification across immunity, microbiome and metabolism, yet existing computational toolkits for these data are mostly borrowed from oncology or generic single-cell workflows [R53]. The conceptual appeal of these syntheses is high; their translational readiness is low, and what the published data do not yet demonstrate is robust, prospective validation of any of the proposed subtyping schemes.

Exosome-based biomarker discovery for cardiovascular disease exemplifies the translational gap most starkly. AI approaches ranging from Random Forest ensembles to graph neural networks integrate EV-derived multi-omics with clinical metadata, with reported AUCs typically between 0.80 and 0.92, yet reproducibility is undermined by non-standardised isolation, pre-analytic variability and small discovery cohorts [R55]. Similar concerns apply to neoantigen pipelines that integrate WGS, transcriptomics and proteomics with convolutional predictors, where portability and external validation remain unresolved despite promising internal performance [R35]. Across these domains, integration platforms often propagate batch effects unless explicit harmonisation, ComBat-style adjustment or domain-adversarial training is applied, and the absence of such steps is rarely reported transparently.

The reproducibility crisis is therefore not a peripheral concern but the central axis around which the field's emerging frontiers must be evaluated. FAIR-packaged, containerised workflows distributed as Research Object Crates offer one route, but adoption outside demonstration case studies remains limited [R11]. Reviews of microbiome multi-omics explicitly call for benchmarked datasets, community-driven standards and harmonised reporting before the next wave of methods can be fairly compared [R54]. Translating this aspiration into practice will require not only better containers and metadata, but structural incentives that reward external validation and penalise incremental architectural re-tweaks that masquerade as methodological breakthroughs.

Practical guidance must be calibrated to the user. Bench biologists and clinical microbiologists seeking reproducible host-microbiome analyses should privilege opinionated, containerised workflows built on shared data classes rather than bespoke scripts; EasyMultiProfiler offers exactly this entry point, leveraging SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment containers with a natural-language-style interface [R1]. For studies combining metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metabolomics in moderate-sized cohorts, EMP provides a credible, well-documented path that minimises engineering burden while remaining extensible through its five-module architecture. Biostatisticians and method-oriented researchers will usually want lower-level access: the MultiAssayExperiment Bioconductor class and its ready-to-analyse TCGA objects remain the most mature substrate for bespoke modelling, and reproducible pipeline orchestrators enable systematic comparison of integration methods [R3, R28]. Computational method developers should treat standardised containers and FAIR packaging as table stakes, since the marginal value of yet another clustering or matrix-factorisation algorithm is rapidly approaching zero without rigorous evaluation against shared benchmark panels [R50]. Clinicians and translational scientists face a different trade-off: in contexts such as inflammatory bowel disease or recurrent pregnancy loss, decision support demands not only multi-omics signatures but also analytical validity, external validation, calibration and action-linked thresholds before any pipeline can be deployed at the bedside [R53, R58].

A short-term roadmap follows directly from the surveyed limitations. First, harmonised data structures — extending the MultiAssayExperiment paradigm into longitudinal, single-cell and microbiome-specific contexts — are the most consequential investment; timeOmics already demonstrates that this framework can be enriched for repeated-measures designs without abandoning interoperability [R20, R28]. Second, FAIR packaging of workflows must become routine: packaging pipelines as FAIR Digital Objects with rich semantic metadata, as illustrated by Nextflow-based case studies, ensures that humans and machines can discover, cite and reuse computational artefacts, and the microbiome community should adopt this convention proactively [R11]. Third, the field needs shared benchmark panels grounded in clinically meaningful endpoints; systematic evaluations of biomarker discovery and clustering methods show that top performers depend strongly on data modality, sample size and biological question, and consensus panels are essential for fair comparison [R4, R46, R50]. Fourth, microbiome-specific extensions — handling compositionality, sparsity, phylogeny and host-microbiome coupling — remain under-served, and the proposed roadmap for standardised microbiome workflows should be operationalised rather than merely endorsed [R54]. Fifth, deep learning methods remain hampered by opaque confidence; uncertainty-aware architectures that quantify predictive variance, such as the Dirichlet-based estimation used in TMODINET, should be adopted as a quality requirement rather than a research luxury [R9].

EasyMultiProfiler should be positioned within this roadmap as a defensible choice for host-microbiome research, particularly for groups that need a stable, reproducible entry point and value the Bioconductor ecosystem. Its modular design and adherence to established container classes are genuine strengths. However, EMP shares the structural limitations of any single workflow: it is not a substitute for dedicated single-cell multi-omics frameworks that excel at vertical integration of RNA, protein and chromatin modalities [R10], nor for spatial-aware platforms linking imaging habitats with molecular profiles [R59], nor for clinical-grade decision-support systems that require regulatory-grade validation, harmonised metadata and prospective calibration [R58]. The evidence on EMP itself does not claim coverage of these domains, and the data presented here do not show that microbiome workflows have yet been stress-tested at clinical-decision scale. The field's most consequential deficit is therefore not the absence of new methods but the absence of standardisation across them. Tool choice should be driven by data modality, cohort size, reproducibility constraints and translational stakes, and the coming years will reward contributors who invest in shared infrastructure — containers, benchmarks, semantic metadata and uncertainty quantification — over those who publish isolated algorithms. A coordinated commitment to these foundations is the shortest route to turning multi-omics from a methodological showcase into a routinely reliable component of biomedical research.
